input.text:
Service Connection

Service connection may be granted for a disability resulting from disease or injury incurred in or aggravated by service. 38 U.S.C. § 1110; 38 C.F.R. § 3.303 (a). Service connection requires competent evidence showing: (1) the existence of a present disability; (2) in-service incurrence or aggravation of a disease or injury; and (3) a causal relationship between the present disability and the disease or injury incurred or aggravated during service. Shedden v. Principi, 381 F.3d 1163, 1167 (Fed. Cir. 2004); see also Caluza v. Brown, 7 Vet. App. 498 (1995).

1. Entitlement to service connection for an acquired psychiatric disorder.

The Veteran asserts that he has an acquired psychiatric disorder that is related to active service. Specifically, the Veteran states that he was stationed in Thailand during the Vietnam War and regularly saw bodies being shipped back to the United States and was stationed in Oman before Operation Desert Storm where the situation was very tense. See May 2014 VA examination report; see also August 2023 Hearing Transcript at 15.

The Board finds the September 2023 private psychiatric evaluation report and accompanying opinion of low probative value. While Dr. Q.A. provides an opinion that the Veteran's depressive disorder began during active service, Dr. Q.A. does not provide a rationale or reconcile the negative evidence of record. See Nieves-Rodriguez v. Peake, 22 Vet. App. 295 (2008); Stefl v. Nicholson, 21 Vet. App. 120, 124 (2007). The Board similarly recognizes the Veteran's competent reports of experiencing depression since active service. 

Accordingly, given the inconsistencies between the Veteran's statements and the findings in the STRs and post-service treatment records, the Board places greater weight on the Veteran's statements made during treatment as opposed to the Veteran's more recent and general lay assertions of experiencing depressive symptoms since active service that are related to events during active service. See Buchanan v. Nicholson, 451 F.3d 1331, 1337 (Fed. Cir. 2006) (Board can consider bias in lay evidence and conflicting statements of the veteran in weighing credibility); Rucker v. Brown, 10 Vet. App. 67, 73 (1997) (statements made to physicians for purposes of diagnosis and treatment are exceptionally trustworthy because the declarant has a strong motive to tell the truth in order to receive proper care). 

Based on the foregoing, the Board finds that the evidence of record persuasively weighs against the claim. As the evidence persuasively weighs against the claim, the benefit of the doubt doctrine is not for application and service connection for an acquired psychiatric disorder is not warranted. 38?U.S.C. §?5107(b);?Lynch v. McDonough, 21 F.4th 776 (Fed. Cir. 2021).

INCREASED DISABILITY RATINGS

Disability ratings are determined by applying the criteria set forth in VA's Schedule for Rating Disabilities, which is based on the average impairment of earning capacity. Individual disabilities are assigned separate diagnostic codes. See 38?U.S.C. §?1155; 38?C.F.R. §?4.1. Where there is a question as to which of two evaluations shall be applied, the higher evaluation will be assigned if the disability picture more nearly approximates the criteria for that rating. Otherwise, the lower rating will be assigned. See 38?C.F.R. §?4.7. Any reasonable doubt regarding a degree of disability will be resolved in favor of the veteran. 38?C.F.R. §?4.3. When the evidence is in relative equipoise, the veteran is accorded the benefit of the doubt. 38?U.S.C. §?5107(b). 

When evaluating musculoskeletal disabilities based on limitation of motion, 38 C.F.R. § 4.40 requires consideration of functional loss caused by pain or other factors listed in that section that could occur during flare-ups or after repeated use and, therefore, not be reflected on range-of-motion testing. 38?C.F.R. §?4.45 requires consideration also be given to less movement than normal, more movement than normal, weakened movement, excess fatigability, incoordination, and pain on movement. See DeLuca v. Brown, 8?Vet. App.?202 (1995); see also Mitchell v. Shinseki, 25?Vet. App.?32, 44 (2011).

The Board acknowledges that the Veteran submitted a medical opinion from a private physician, Dr. R.T., in October 2023. The physician noted the Veteran's complaints of being unable to walk a quarter of a mile without resting, significant left knee swelling, difficulty climbing stairs, his knee grinding and coming out of the joint, and left knee stiffness. The Veteran also reported that he falls 2-3 times a year. The Veteran reported similar symptoms during his hearing testimony in August 2023. Dr. R.T. stated that the Veteran's left knee disability would be more appropriately rated at 50-75 percent.

While the Board acknowledges the Veteran's competent complaints of experiencing left knee instability, the rating criteria under Diagnostic Code 5257 requires a diagnosis of a left knee ligament tear or left knee patellofemoral complex disability. No such diagnosis is of record. Moreover, Dr. R.T.'s conclusory statement that the Veteran's left knee should be rated as 50 to 75 percent disabling is deemed to be of no probative value. The Board notes that there is no possibility of receiving a 75 percent disability rating under the VA rating schedule and the private physician does not provide any explanation for his statement.

In conclusion, the evidence persuasively weighs against the Veteran's claim for a rating in excess of 10 percent for the service-connected left knee degenerative joint disease for the entire appeal period. As the evidence persuasively weighs against the claim, the benefit of the doubt doctrine is not for application and the claim is denied. 38?U.S.C. §?5107(b);?Lynch v. McDonough, 21 F.4th 776 (Fed. Cir. 2021)..

1. Entitlement to TDIU prior to October 9, 2019.

The Veteran seeks entitlement to a TDIU prior to October 9, 2019.

TDIU is a form of increased rating claim, and the effective date rules for increased compensation apply. See Norris v. West, 12 Vet. App. 413 (1999).

A total rating for compensation purposes may be assigned where the schedular rating is less than total, when it is found that the disabled person is unable to secure or follow a substantially gainful occupation as a result of a single service-connected disability ratable at 60 percent or more. 38 U.S.C. § 1155; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.340, 3.341, 4.16(a).

In order to establish entitlement to TDIU due to service-connected disabilities, there must be impairment so severe that it is impossible for the average person to secure and follow a substantially gainful occupation. 38 U.S.C. § 1155; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.340, 3.341, 4.16. In reaching such a determination, the central inquiry is "whether the Veteran's service-connected disabilities alone are of sufficient severity to produce unemployability." Hatlestad v. Brown, 5 Vet. App. 524, 529 (1993). Consideration may be given to the Veteran's level of education, special training, and previous work experience when arriving at this conclusion, but factors such as age or impairment caused by non-service-connected disabilities are not to be considered. 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.341, 4.16, 4.19; Van Hoose v. Brown, 4 Vet. App. 361, 363 (1993).

The Board finds that entitlement to TDIU is warranted for the period beginning August 2018 to prior to October 9, 2019.  

Initially, the Board finds that the Veteran meets the schedular criteria for the award of TDIU during the entire period for consideration. The Veteran is in receipt of at an evaluation over 40 percent for a single disability (both posttraumatic stress disorder and right foot fractures) and has additional disabilities that bring the Veteran's combined rating to 70 percent.

In a VA examination in September 2018 the Veteran was noted to have been employed in the OR as an operating room specialist. However, his physical problems precluded him from standing for long periods of time. As a result, he was not working. It was not known if the leg will eventually be cured or normal. 

Affording the Veteran the benefit of the doubt, the TDIU is warranted for the period beginning August 2018. As noted above, the Veteran meets the schedular criteria for assignment of a TDIU beginning no later than August 2018. The Veteran, via his representative, filed an intent to file a claim in April 2019 and followed up with a claim for TDIU in October 2019. Therefore, the Board will ascertain whether there is any evidence of unemployability in the year prior to April 2019. The Veteran reported in October 2019 that he was last full time employed in August 2018 and that he was last employed in January 2019. Based upon the Veteran's limited education, limited work experience, and the physical nature of the work he has experience in, the Board finds that the Veteran's service-connected disabilities render the Veteran unemployable. Affording the Veteran the benefit of the doubt, the Veteran's employment from August 2018 to January 2019 was not substantially gainful.
